basic_information.official_title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING SUPPLEMENTAL FUNDS FOR THE OPERATION OF THE BANGSAMORO GOVERNMENT AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
signed_by: Jaime M. Ayub, Director III, OIC-Secretary-General
basic_information.effectivity: 15 days after publication in any newspaper of general circulation in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: An ₱11.3 billion top-up to the 2025 regional budget, funded from Treasury investment income and unspent money from earlier years. More than a third of it — ₱4.02 billion — sits in a Contingent Fund released at the Chief Minister's discretion.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: Investment income and unutilised prior-year appropriations had accumulated in the Bangsamoro Treasury. This act redistributes ₱11.3 billion of them across 23 agencies and 2 special purpose funds.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: ₱4.02 billion goes into a Contingent Fund covering digitalisation, Islamic finance and the acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank. The Office of the Chief Minister receives ₱1.50 billion, agriculture ₱1.27 billion, and the Parliament appropriates ₱400 million to itself. Funds run to 31 December 2026.
who_will_be_affected: Households receiving TABANG assistance and AMBaG medical aid
Farmers and fisherfolk, through ₱1.27 billion in agriculture support
Families needing housing, through ₱720.8 million in human settlements
Disaster-affected communities, through ₱503.7 million in rapid emergency response
Madaris learners and scholars, through ₱447.2 million in education
Marawi residents, through a ₱17.3 million rehabilitation line
citizen_summary.when_will_it_take_effect: In force since 2025 — approved by the Chief Minister on 16 June 2025, effective 15 days after publication. Funds run to 31 December 2026, with Personnel Services expiring 31 December 2025.

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: NOW LAW. ₱11.3 billion of Treasury investment income and previously unspent money. The single largest item is not a ministry at all — it is a ₱4.02 billion Contingent Fund released only on the Chief Minister's approval.
in_practice: ₱11,300,000,000 total across 23 agencies plus 2 special purpose funds
Funded from income generated on Bureau of the Treasury investments and unutilised prior years' appropriations
Contingent Fund: ₱4.02 billion — 35.6% of the act
Office of the Chief Minister: ₱1.50 billion, including ₱507.5 million for TABANG and ₱111 million for AMBaG medical assistance
Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform: ₱1.27 billion
Human Settlements and Development: ₱720.8 million, almost entirely capital outlay
Interior and Local Government: ₱715.4 million, including ₱503.7 million for rapid emergency disaster response
The Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament appropriated ₱400 million to itself, all operating expenses
Funds are available for release and disbursement until 31 December 2026; Personnel Services only until 31 December 2025

for_specific_groups.Households in need: ₱507,543,622 for Tulong Alay sa Bangsamorong Nangangailangan (TABANG) and ₱21,824,000 for Strengthening Access to Living Assistance to Marginalized Bangsamoro (SALAM), both through the Office of the Chief Minister.
for_specific_groups.Patients: ₱111,000,000 for Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government (AMBaG), plus ₱462.4 million at the health ministry including ₱145.0 million for medical outreach and ₱52.4 million for nutrition.
for_specific_groups.Farmers and fisherfolk: ₱1,268,850,019, of which ₱1.19 billion for Basic Integration for Harmonized Intervention — including ₱447.6 million in machinery and equipment and ₱119.4 million in transportation equipment.
for_specific_groups.Families needing housing: ₱720,805,789 at the human settlements ministry, ₱702.0 million of it capital outlay including ₱566.8 million in infrastructure assets.
for_specific_groups.Madaris learners and scholars: ₱148.3 million for Madaris Education Services, ₱110.4 million for technical-vocational provisions and ₱100.6 million for the Access to Higher and Modern Education Scholarship Program.
for_specific_groups.Marawi residents: ₱17,274,114 for the Marawi Rehabilitation Program, under the Office of the Chief Minister.
for_specific_groups.Settler communities: ₱5,000,000 is set aside within the Contingent Fund exclusively for a General Assembly to be conducted by the Office for Settler Communities.
for_specific_groups.Indigenous peoples: ₱2,250,000 for Indigenous Peoples' Development Initiatives — 0.02% of the act, the smallest ministry allocation in it.
for_specific_groups.Conflict-affected communities: ₱206.3 million for public order and safety, including ₱160.4 million for peacebuilding initiatives and ₱13.2 million for Sustaining Journey to Peace.

what_this_means_for_you.where_this_applies: The whole BARMM, with funds released directly to ministries, offices and agencies including their provincial offices.
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: Release and disbursement run to 31 December 2026; Personnel Services expired 31 December 2025.
what_you_can_do: Check ministry websites for infrastructure project disclosures required within 30 days of contract and of completion
Look for quarterly financial and physical accomplishment reports on the Contingent Fund, which must be published on the implementing agency's website
Ask your LGU or the social services ministry about TABANG, AMBaG and SALAM assistance
If reports are missing, note that officials' salaries are automatically suspended until they comply
watch_out_for: ₱4.02 billion — 35.6% of the act — sits in a Contingent Fund released solely on the Chief Minister's approval, with stated uses that include 'other expenditures' covering unforeseen initiatives not otherwise in the act.

The Parliament appropriated ₱400 million to itself, entirely operating expenses, including ₱80 million in representation expenses, ₱46.7 million in travel and ₱213.3 million in unspecified 'other maintenance and operating expenses'.
The Office of the Chief Minister's ₱1.50 billion includes ₱404.2 million in representation expenses and ₱327.9 million in professional and consultancy services.
This is the second of 3 supplementals funded from unspent money — ₱8.44 billion for 2024, ₱11.3 billion for 2025 and ₱16.83 billion for 2026. The amount grows each year.
The Ministry of Indigenous Peoples' Affairs received ₱2.25 million, less than the Office of the Wali's ₱10 million and a fraction of the Sports Commission's ₱52 million.

key_terms_explained.Supplemental appropriation: A budget law passed during the year adding to what the annual appropriations act provided.
key_terms_explained.Contingent Fund: A reserve for new or urgent projects arising during the year, released case by case on the Chief Minister's approval.
key_terms_explained.TABANG: Tulong Alay sa Bangsamorong Nangangailangan — an assistance programme run from the Office of the Chief Minister.
key_terms_explained.AMBaG: Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government — medical assistance.
key_terms_explained.SALAM: Strengthening Access to Living Assistance to Marginalized Bangsamoro.
key_terms_explained.KAPYANAN: Kapayapaan sa Pamayanan — a community peace programme.
key_terms_explained.Representation expenses: Spending on official entertainment, meetings and hospitality.
key_terms_explained.Al-Amanah Islamic Bank: Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines, the country's only Islamic bank. The Contingent Fund may cover the cost of acquiring it.
key_terms_explained.Cash budgeting system: Appropriations valid only within a fixed window, after which they lapse and unobligated balances revert.

what_this_means_for_you.status_note: Passed 29 May 2025 and approved by the Chief Minister on 16 June 2025. The enacted copy is attested by an OIC-Secretary-General rather than the Secretary-General.

limitations: More than a third of the act is discretionary reserve rather than programmed spending.
Personnel Services expired on 31 December 2025 and the rest on 31 December 2026.
The act funds programmes, not entitlements.
Some of the largest object lines — representation expenses and 'other operating expenses' — are not itemised further.

for_citizens: None. An appropriations act imposes no duty on the public.
for_agencies: Secure a Special Allotment Release Order before obligating appropriations
Obtain a Certification of Availability of Funds from the chief accountant before incurring any obligation, made part of the signed contract
Obtain the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle before procuring transportation equipment
For Contingent Fund releases, submit indicative programme plans, construction plans and programme of works, an indicative procurement plan, a cost-benefit analysis and a list of beneficiaries
Release Personnel Benefit Fund money for new positions only once posts are filled and appointment, assumption, oath, service record and deployment documents are submitted
Submit quarterly financial and physical accomplishment reports within 30 days of each quarter's end, published on the agency website for Contingent Fund items
Submit a status report on Commission on Audit findings within 60 days of the annual audit report and post it on the agency website
Post infrastructure project details, winning contractor, actual cost and variation orders within 30 days

what_is_prohibited: Incurring an obligation without first securing a Certification of Availability of Funds from the agency's chief accountant.
Procuring transportation equipment without the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle.
Releasing Personnel Benefit Fund money for newly created positions before those positions are actually filled and the supporting documents submitted.

Treating funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies, or to LGUs as disbursed before the goods, works or services have actually been delivered, inspected and accepted within the validity period.
Deducting engineering and administrative overhead above 1%, or administrative costs above 3%, of project costs for projects over ₱1,000,000.
Obligating appropriations after the validity period.

penalties.for_citizens: None. The act creates no offence.
penalties.for_officials: Failure to submit the required financial and physical accountability reports results in the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until compliance. Repeated failure or refusal without justifiable cause may be a ground for administrative disciplinary action under civil service rules.

where_to_complain.first_stop: The ministry, office or agency implementing the programme or project
where_to_complain.oversight: Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management; the Speaker; and Parliament's Committee on Finance, Budget and Management
where_to_complain.audit: The Commission on Audit, whose annual audit report each agency must answer within 60 days
where_to_complain.note: Contingent Fund releases require the Chief Minister's approval on the finance ministry's recommendation, supported by a list of beneficiaries and a cost-benefit analysis.

everyday_scenarios: A family receives medical assistance from the regional government. ₱111 million was appropriated here for AMBaG through the Office of the Chief Minister.
A farmers' cooperative receives machinery. ₱447.6 million in machinery and equipment was appropriated under the agriculture ministry's BINHI programme.
A displaced family is resettled. ₱720.8 million went to human settlements, ₱566.8 million of it in infrastructure assets.
A resident wants to know what a project cost. Section 13 requires the agency to post the detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 days of the completion certificate.
A ministry stops filing accountability reports. Section 12 automatically suspends the salaries of the responsible officials until they comply.

key_provisions: Section 1 — Appropriation of Funds, made “out of the income generated from the investments made to the Bureau of Treasury, and unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury”. Agency totals for the FY 2025 supplemental appropriation: the Office of the Chief Minister ₱1,501,002,314; Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform ₱1,268,850,019; Human Settlements and Development ₱720,805,789; the Interior and Local Government ₱715,363,470; Health ₱462,375,700; Basic, Higher and Technical Education ₱447,156,203; Public Works ₱425,913,400; the Bangsamoro Transition Authority ₱400,000,000; Transportation and Communications ₱399,777,350; Social Services and Development ₱229,478,100; Public Order and Safety ₱206,341,632; Labor and Employment ₱200,937,023; Science and Technology ₱85,094,521; the Bangsamoro Sports Commission ₱52,000,000; Environment, Natural Resources and Energy ₱39,900,000; the Cooperatives and Social Enterprise Authority ₱24,000,000; the Bangsamoro Women Commission ₱23,779,700; the Office of the Wali ₱10,000,000; the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage ₱8,794,045; the Bangsamoro Board of Investments ₱8,702,767; Indigenous Peoples' Affairs ₱2,250,000; the Bangsamoro Youth Commission ₱2,000,000; and Trade, Investment and Tourism ₱835,500. Two special purpose funds follow: the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund ₱41,914,262 and the Contingent Fund ₱4,022,728,205 — a total of ₱11,300,000,000.

Section 1 (programme detail) — The Office of the Chief Minister's ₱1.50 billion covers Policy Formulation and Development ₱582,506,657, Tulong Alay sa Bangsamorong Nangangailangan ₱507,543,622, General Management and Supervision ₱166,048,734, Ayudang Medikal mula sa Bangsamoro Government ₱111,000,000, Management of Library and Archives Services ₱29,576,604, Strengthening Access to Living Assistance to Marginalized Bangsamoro ₱21,824,000, Kapayapaan sa Pamayanan ₱20,956,378, the Marawi Rehabilitation Program ₱17,274,114, Support to Local Moral Governance ₱12,500,000, Promotion of the Welfare of Bangsamoro Communities Outside the Region ₱6,975,866, and conflict resolution and reconciliation mechanisms ₱6,282,846. By object, it includes ₱611,000,000 in financial assistance and subsidy, ₱404,166,600 in representation expenses, ₱292,445,813 in professional services and ₱35,465,340 in consultancy services. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority's ₱400,000,000 is entirely maintenance and operating expenses, split into a Legislation Program ₱253,332,800, a Representation Program ₱103,333,600 and an Oversight Program ₱43,333,600, and by object into ₱213,332,800 other operating expenses, ₱80,000,000 representation expenses, ₱60,000,000 financial assistance and subsidy and ₱46,667,200 travelling expenses.

Special Provisions, Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund — The ₱41,914,262 covers personnel services for newly created positions as additional staff complement for the Legal and Legislative Liaison Division and the Provincial Social Welfare Office in the Special Geographic Area under the social services ministry, for the Offices of the Deputy Speakers and Deputy Floor Leaders under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, and for other newly created positions. Funds are released only when the positions are actually filled and on submission of appointment, certification of assumption to duty, oath of office, service record and deployment order.

Special Provisions, Contingent Fund — The ₱4,022,728,205 covers new or urgent projects and activities needing implementation or payment during the year, including the digitalization of the BARMM bureaucracy; a Transitional Development Impact Fund; Islamic Finance Programs, subject to Section 29 of BAA 65, the FY 2025 General Appropriations Act; “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs”; customs duties and taxes including tax expenditures and assumed tax payable on foreign assistance and donations such as Japan Government Assistance; infrastructure necessary for establishing the Bangsamoro Government Center; ₱5,000,000 exclusively for the General Assembly to be conducted by the Office for Settler Communities; and other expenditures supporting programmes mandated by law, including unforeseen initiatives not covered by the act. Release is subject to the Chief Minister's approval on the finance ministry's recommendation after technical assessment and review of indicative programme plans, construction plans and programme of works, indicative procurement plan, cost-benefit analysis and list of beneficiaries. Quarterly reports must be submitted and published on the implementing agency's website.

Sections 2–8 (General Provisions) — A Special Allotment Release Order authorises agencies to obligate appropriations; government funds must be used as authorised; agencies must strictly adhere to existing procurement laws; engineering and administrative overhead not exceeding 1% of project funds and administrative costs not exceeding 3% of project costs may be deducted for projects over ₱1,000,000; all transportation equipment outlays require the Chief Minister's Authority to Purchase Motor Vehicle on the finance ministry's recommendation; and no obligation may be incurred without a Certification of Availability of Funds from the agency's chief accountant, made part of the signed contract.

Section 9 — Cash Budgeting System. Appropriations are available for release and disbursement until 31 December 2026, except Personnel Services which are valid for obligation and disbursement only until 31 December 2025. After the validity period unreleased appropriations lapse and unobligated funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. Funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies, or to local government units are not considered disbursed until actually used to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period.

Sections 10–15 — Funds are released directly to ministries, offices and agencies including their provincial offices and organisational units. Agencies must submit a status report on Commission on Audit findings within 60 days of the annual audit report, furnishing copies to the finance ministry, the Speaker and Parliament's Committee on Finance, Budget and Management, and posting it on the agency website. Financial and physical accountability reports must be submitted monthly, quarterly or yearly in hardcopy, electronically and on the agency website, with failure resulting in automatic suspension of the responsible officials' salaries until compliance and repeated failure a ground for administrative disciplinary action. Transparency in Infrastructure Projects requires posting the project title, location and description, the estimates behind the Approved Budget for the Contract and the winning contractor with awarded bid estimates within 30 calendar days of entering the contract, and the detailed actual cost with any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion. A separability clause follows, and the act takes effect 15 days after publication.

related_legislation.related_note: Supplements BAA 65, the FY 2025 General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, whose Section 29 governs the Islamic finance programmes funded from the Contingent Fund. It sits between BAA 63, the FY 2024 supplemental at ₱8.44 billion, and BAA 91, the FY 2026 supplemental at ₱16.83 billion — all 3 funded from unspent prior-year appropriations. Reversion of unobligated funds follows Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. The cash budgeting system and automatic salary suspension mirror Sections 35 and 75 of BAA 84, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025.

citizen_questions.q: How much is this, and where did the money come from?
citizen_questions.a: ₱11,300,000,000, appropriated out of income generated on Bureau of the Treasury investments and unutilised prior years' appropriations held in the Bangsamoro Treasury.
The Contingent Fund, at ₱4,022,728,205 — 35.6% of the act. It is not allocated to any programme in advance; releases require the Chief Minister's approval on the finance ministry's recommendation.

citizen_questions.q: What can the Contingent Fund be spent on?
citizen_questions.a: Digitalising the BARMM bureaucracy, a Transitional Development Impact Fund, Islamic finance programmes, the cost of acquiring Al-Amanah Islamic Bank, customs duties and taxes on foreign assistance including Japanese aid, infrastructure for the Bangsamoro Government Center, ₱5 million for a General Assembly of settler communities, and other expenditures including unforeseen initiatives not covered by the act.

Yes — ₱400,000,000 to the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, entirely maintenance and operating expenses. By object it comprises ₱213.3 million in other operating expenses, ₱80 million in representation expenses, ₱60 million in financial assistance and subsidy and ₱46.7 million in travelling expenses.

citizen_questions.q: How long was the money available?
citizen_questions.a: Until 31 December 2026 for release and disbursement, except Personnel Services which expired on 31 December 2025. Unreleased appropriations lapsed and unobligated funds reverted to the Treasury.

citizen_questions.q: How does this compare with other supplementals?
citizen_questions.a: It is the middle of 3. BAA 63 appropriated ₱8.44 billion for FY 2024, this act ₱11.3 billion for FY 2025, and BAA 91 ₱16.83 billion for FY 2026 — ₱36.57 billion in total, all of it money earlier budgets had not spent.

views.simple: An ₱11.3 billion supplemental budget for 2025, funded from Bureau of the Treasury investment income and prior years' unspent appropriations. The largest single item is a ₱4.02 billion Contingent Fund released on the Chief Minister's approval, covering bureaucratic digitalisation, Islamic finance and the acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank. The Office of the Chief Minister takes ₱1.50 billion including TABANG and AMBaG assistance, agriculture ₱1.27 billion, human settlements ₱720.8 million, and the Parliament ₱400 million for itself. Funds ran to 31 December 2026.
